digest.intro: Infrastructure breaks, targets shift, and software eats itself from within.

items.title: Musk, Not Trump, Ordered the Starlink Throttle That Blinded Ukraine's Drones
items.blurb: The WSJ nailed down that Musk personally set a 160 kph speed cap on Starshield terminals, rendering Ukrainian offensive and interceptor drones effectively useless — then let Trump publicly absorb the blame. The structural story here isn't Musk's motive; it's that a single person's discretion now constitutes a choke point in a sovereign nation's air defense. That's not a political story, it's an infrastructure story.

items.title: The UN Formally Abandoned 1.5°C — The New Plan Requires Removing Hundreds of Gigatonnes of CO₂
items.blurb: UNEP's new framing isn't about hitting a limit anymore — it's about minimizing how long and how far we exceed it, which means dramatic emissions cuts now plus the removal of hundreds of gigatonnes of carbon before 2100. The best-case scenario they're now modeling is 1.8°C with massive, not-yet-proven carbon removal technology doing real work. The goalpost didn't move; the game changed.

items.title: Nigeria Reports First Ebola Case in Over a Decade as an Active Outbreak Tops 4,600 Dead
items.blurb: A fourth African nation has now confirmed cases from the current outbreak, which has killed more than 4,600 people. This is the kind of story that arrives quietly and then suddenly isn't quiet. Worth knowing before it's everywhere.

sections.heading: The software supply chain eats itself

items.title: LiteLLM 1.107.0 Was a Credential Stealer Disguised as an AI Developer Library
items.blurb: The compromised release placed a `.pth` file in site-packages that ran a credential harvester on every Python process startup — whether or not you ever imported litellm — collecting SSH keys, cloud credentials, CI/CD secrets, browser passwords, and LLM provider API keys, then encrypted and exfiltrated them. A background daemon phoned home every hour for new instructions. LiteLLM is foundational plumbing in the AI agent stack, which makes this a meaningful signal about the attack surface the whole ecosystem is building on.

items.title: Eight Certificate Authority Private Keys Leaked — eMudhra Exits the SSL Business
items.blurb: eMudhra, a CA trusted by Mozilla, Microsoft, and Apple, had private keys for eight intermediate certificate authorities compromised and is now exiting the SSL/TLS business entirely. They say no end-entity certificates were issued from the affected CAs and the breach was contained within 14 hours, but a root-of-trust failure at this level — regardless of scope — is the kind of thing that quietly matters. The web's trust infrastructure depends on a surprisingly small number of these actors.

items.title: A 360M Model That Pretends to Be a Terminal — No Shell, No Filesystem, Just Prediction
items.blurb: One developer fine-tuned Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B on recorded terminal sessions so it predicts screen-state changes frame by frame — you type `pythoon` and it autocorrects like a real shell would, creates files, runs vim and tmux, plays Snake, and holds state for a few commands. It runs in-browser via WebGPU at 208 MB. The deeper question it opens: what's the line between software that's written and software that's learned, and does it matter if you can't tell the difference from the outside?

items.title: Switch 2 Jailbreak: A Solo Researcher Cracked Nintendo's Latest Hardware in Two Weeks
items.blurb: The first software-only tethered jailbreak for the Switch 2 landed, written up in the obsessive how-I-broke-this genre that never gets old. The researcher used a WebKit exploit as the entry vector (a reliable console jailbreak surface), built a hardware harness so an AI agent could attempt it autonomously via JetKVM controller inputs, and then Mario Kart World got modded in a single day of vibing as a proof of capability. The write-up is the artifact.

items.title: Scientists Turned an 80-Year-Old's Blood Cells Into Neural Stem Cells With a Molecular Age Under 20
items.blurb: Researchers at University Hospital Bonn reprogrammed immature red blood cells from an octogenarian into neural stem cells — cells that can eventually develop into brain cells — and found that molecular aging markers had reset to under 20 years. Crucially, the rejuvenation happened gradually, letting them observe the process in real time rather than just before and after. The paper is in Aging Cell; it's in-lab and early, but the ability to track the reset step-by-step is what's genuinely new here.

items.title: What Happened When Bhutan — the Last Country to Ban TV — Finally Turned It On
items.blurb: In 1999, Bhutan became the last country in the world to legalize television, and Aeon's documentary treatment of what happened next is essentially a controlled experiment in how mass media rewires culture, identity, and social behavior — compressed into one society, one moment. The before/after is unusually clean for that kind of question. Reliable Aeon signal for anyone curious about how communication tools reshape the people who use them.

facts.fact: The Starlink speed cap Musk set — 160 kph — is slow enough that many Ukrainian drones equipped with Starshield simply can't fly at normal operational speed without losing their data connection.
The malicious LiteLLM 1.107.0 credential stealer ran on every Python process startup on the infected machine — not just when litellm was imported — by abusing Python's `.pth` file loading mechanism.
University of Bonn researchers reversed more than 60 years of molecular aging in human cells by converting an 80-year-old's blood cells into neural stem cells with an age signature of under 20.

The WorldTUI terminal model runs entirely in-browser via WebGPU at 208 MB, with no shell or filesystem behind it — every screen update is purely the model predicting the next most likely character grid.
UNEP's new best-case climate scenario requires humanity to remove hundreds of gigatonnes of CO₂ from the atmosphere before 2100 — technology that does not yet exist at meaningful scale.

make_something.prompt: Build a 'world model' for a constrained system you know well — not a terminal, but something else with a small, learnable state space: a chess position, a single webpage's DOM, a specific hardware interface. Sketch (on paper or in code) what training data you'd need, what the input/output format would be, and what 'repair' training would look like. The point isn't to build the thing — it's to notice where the edges of learnability are in a system you thought you understood.

art_picks.title: Playtime
art_picks.creator: Jacques Tati
art_picks.why: A film that IS a system: Tati built a full-scale city (Tativille) and then filmed the chaos of modern architecture eating human behavior alive. Every frame is a generative composition — you direct your own gaze across an endlessly tiled world where the joke is always structural, never personal. For someone building interactive environments, it's the deepest possible meditation on how designed space shapes behavior without anyone noticing.

art_picks.title: The Poetics of Space (paintings and objects)
art_picks.creator: Joseph Cornell
art_picks.why: Cornell went unreasonably, obsessively deep on one thing: the shadow-box as portal. Each work is a closed system — a cosmology made from junk, astrology charts, Victorian ephemera, and bird cages — that somehow produces genuine longing. The physical/digital edge doesn't get more surgically explored than when a man spends 40 years building miniature universes in a basement in Queens.

art_picks.title: Remain in Light
art_picks.creator: Talking Heads
art_picks.why: Brian Eno and David Byrne's 1980 masterpiece treats the band as a generative system: interlocking rhythmic loops, polyrhythm borrowed from West African music, and lyrics that read like someone trying to describe consciousness from outside the skull. The surface is ecstatic funk; the deep structure is a treatise on how identity fragments under modernity. Still no better model for expressive, playful work with serious architecture underneath.

events.name: Hiroko Ohno: Event Horizon
events.venue: Amos Eno Gallery, 191 Henry Street, Lower East Side
events.why: The title alone earns attention — a solo show by a painter using cosmological language to frame intimate scale work; small LES gallery, no institutional noise.

events.name: Synthesize Me: Olga Titus & Michael Dickey
events.why: A two-person show at a small gallery whose very name (IRL) flags the physical/digital tension — Titus and Dickey working in and around materiality and synthetic process, exactly the edge where Willem's own practice lives.

events.name: The Surrealist Book: Tomorrow Lives in Mirrors
events.why: Rare Surrealist artists' books treated as art objects — glass-bound manifestos, solarized photo-poems, sculptural bindings — built around the newly gifted Zell Collection; the show argues the book was the movement's most radical medium, which is a very different and more interesting claim than another paintings survey.

events.name: Jeff Tweedy Solo (with Case Oats)
events.venue: The Town Hall, 123 West 43rd Street, Manhattan
events.why: Tweedy supporting his triple album Twilight Override — a songwriter who treats the album format as a serious structural object — solo and stripped at a 1,500-seat historic room that's exactly the right size for this; the opener Case Oats is his son Spencer Tweedy and Casey Gomez, which makes the whole evening a strange family mythology.

events.name: Salon Art + Design (15th Edition)
events.venue: Park Avenue Armory, 643 Park Avenue, Manhattan
events.why: 50+ international galleries across collectible furniture, ceramics, lighting, sculpture, and jewelry inside the Armory's vast drill hall — the entrance this year reimagined by Courtney McLeod as a surrealist Alice-in-Wonderland scheme called 'Impossible Blooms'; it's where the serious object world overlaps with design-as-culture, and it's the best room in New York for it.
